title: Questions & Answers on the AI Act

evidence.quote: Providers of high-risk AI systems need to carry out a risk assessment and design the system in a way that risks to health, safety and fundamental rights are minimised.
Providers of models with systemic risk must assess and mitigate these risks
Before placing a high-risk AI system on the EU market or otherwise putting it into service, providers must subject it to a conformity assessment.
The AI Act obliges providers of such models to document technical information about the models, and to disclose certain information to downstream system providers.
High-risk systems will also need to be trained and tested with sufficiently representative datasets... They must also be traceable and auditable, ensuring that appropriate documentation is kept
Providers of high-risk AI systems remain responsible for the safety and compliance of the system throughout its lifecycle. Where necessary, they have to report and respond to serious incidents
conducting state-of-the-art model evaluations, reporting serious incidents, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity
evidence.source_section: General-purpose AI models with systemic risk

evidence.quote: The AI Act introduces specific transparency requirements for providers and deployers of certain interactive or generative AI systems (including chatbots or deep fakes).
Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risks additionally have to assess and mitigate systemic risks
Deployers need to assign human oversight to a person in their organisation. That person or persons must be sufficiently equipped and enabled to exercise human oversight.
Depending on the type of high-risk AI system, the conformity assessment may have to be conducted by an independent conformity assessment body.
To enable supervision and ensure public transparency, providers of high-risk AI systems have to register the system in a public EU database.
Providers of generative AI systems need to mark the AI outputs in a machine-readable format and ensure they are detectable as artificially generated or manipulated.
conducting state-of-the-art model evaluations, reporting serious incidents, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity of their models
evidence.source_section: General-purpose AI models with systemic risk

evidence.quote: Up to €35m or 7% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year (whichever is higher) for infringements on prohibited practices or non-compliance related to requirements on data
Up to €15m or 3% of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year for non-compliance with any of the other requirements
Before placing a high-risk AI system on the EU market or otherwise putting it into service, providers must subject it to a conformity assessment.

national competent authorities are responsible for overseeing and enforcing rules for AI systems, while the AI Office is responsible for governing and enforcing the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
they have to report and respond to serious incidents, take corrective actions in case of identified risks or non-compliance, provide information and cooperate with market surveillance authorities
The GPAI Code of Practice is a voluntary tool, prepared by independent experts in a multi-stakeholder process, designed to help industry comply with the AI Act's obligations

policy_extraction.implementation_notes: This document is a Q&A/FAQ published by the European Commission explaining the EU AI Act (Regulation). The underlying AI Act is binding law; this document itself is regulatory guidance/explanatory material. Application dates are phased: prohibitions from 2 Feb 2025, GPAI rules from 2 Aug 2025, high-risk rules from 2 Aug 2026 (potentially delayed per Digital Omnibus proposal), Annex II products from 2 Aug 2027. The GPAI Code of Practice is voluntary but can serve as a compliance demonstration tool.

risk_framing.rationale_summary: The document repeatedly centers fundamental rights as the primary justification for regulation, banning specific AI practices because they 'contravene EU values because they violate fundamental rights,' requiring fundamental rights impact assessments, and structuring the risk classification around the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights. Consumer/public safety is a strong secondary frame, as health and safety risks are co-stated throughout. Innovation enablement and economic competitiveness appear as secondary justifications to show the regulation is balanced. Existential/systemic risk language appears specifically around GPAI models (CBRN attacks, loss of human control) but is not the dominant framing.

evidence_spans.quote: It aims to address risks to health, safety and fundamental rights.
a very limited set of particularly harmful uses of AI systems that contravene EU values because they violate fundamental rights and will therefore be banned

The AI Act considers a limited number of AI systems as high-risk, because they potentially create an adverse impact on people's safety or their fundamental rights (as protected by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights)
powerful models could enable chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear (CBRN) attacks or large-scale sophisticated cyberattacks, escape human control
deployers that are bodies governed by public law...shall perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights
